Happy to. Here's the quick version, in table form:

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Assessed value | The value the county puts on a property for tax purposes. It is what the tax bill is calculated from. |
| Base year value | The value set when a property is purchased or newly constructed. It is the starting point for later assessments. |
| Supplemental assessment | An extra assessment triggered mid-year by a change in ownership or new construction, covering the difference between the old and new value for the rest of that year. |
| Prop 8 decline-in-value | A temporary reduction when the market value falls below the factored base year value. It is reviewed every year and can be restored as the market recovers. |
| Exclusion | A change in ownership or use that does not trigger reassessment, such as certain transfers between family members. Exact rules depend on your jurisdiction and the training module. |
| Appeal roll | The list of properties where the owner has formally disputed the assessed value and the case is pending a hearing. |

The exact definitions in your software module may be worded differently, so check them against the module text. Ready? Question 1: A home sells in March. Which value is set at that point, and what does it become the starting point for?

**Camera drops when the microwave runs**
Microwaves put out noise on the 2.4 GHz band, which many baby cameras use.
1. In your router settings, move the camera to the 5 GHz band if it supports it. If not, move the router or camera farther from the microwave.
2. If the camera is on 2.4 GHz, change the router's channel to 1 or 11. Channel 6 is closest to what microwaves interfere with.
3. Move the router so it isn't in the same line as the kitchen, or add a cheap Wi-Fi extender near the nursery.
4. Quick test: run the microwave for 30 seconds and watch the feed.

**Tracker not showing the other entries**
1. Make sure you're connected to the internet, then pull down to refresh or force-close and reopen the app.
2. Check that the app is updated, and that your phone's background data and battery saver aren't blocking sync.
3. In the app's sharing or family settings, confirm that Hana's and your mom's accounts are still linked to the same baby profile. A common cause is that they're logging to a duplicate profile.
4. If it still lags, log out and back in. Your data stays on the server.

**Summary tab and export**

5:24 am update. did the 2 a.m. feed and then couldn't get back to sleep, so now i'm editing a thanksgiving text instead of resting like a functional adult 🙃 can you tighten this up? it's going to hana's parents and my mom, we're hosting at our place on the 27th, potluck style.

"hi all! thanksgiving is thursday nov 27 at our place (209). we'd love to do it potluck. here's what i'm thinking: hana's mom - sides, hana's dad - dessert, judith - cranberry sauce and rolls. i'll do the turkey, probably. please let me know if that works!! also theo will be 4 months so dinner might get interrupted by crying, sorry in advance"

Happy to help, and sorry the night got cut short. Here's a tightened version:

"Hi all! Thanksgiving is Thursday, Nov 27, at our place (209), potluck style. Here's the plan:

• Hana's mom: sides
• Hana's dad: dessert
• Judith: cranberry sauce and rolls
• Me: turkey

Please reply if that works or you'd like to swap. Fair warning: Theo may interrupt dinner with some commentary. See you all then!"

I cut the double apology and the "probably" on the turkey so it reads as confident. Want me to add arrival time or dietary notes?

yes please add a line: no cilantro in anything, and decaf after noon, that's for my mom. and one more thing, can you reword the assignments so my mom ends up with dishes she makes at her own place and brings over? like the rolls and cranberry sauce could be done at her condo. i just don't want people cooking in my kitchen on thursday, it's tiny. but i don't want to say that part to her

Sure. Since the text says what people bring, framing the dishes as make-ahead handles it without singling anyone out. Here's the revised version:

"Hi all! Thanksgiving is Thursday, Nov 27, at our place (209), potluck style. To keep things easy, please bring dishes made ahead and ready to serve:

• Hana's mom: sides
• Hana's dad: dessert
• Judith: cranberry sauce and rolls (a perfect make-at-home, bring-warm kind of dish)
• Me: turkey

Two small notes: no cilantro in anything, please, and we'll have decaf on hand for after noon.

Reply if that works or you want to swap. Fair warning, Theo may interrupt dinner with some commentary. Can't wait to see everyone!"

The "made ahead" line applies to everyone, so it reads as a general plan rather than a request aimed at one person. If you'd like, I can add a time for arrival, like [arrival time], or a placeholder for oven space so people know what to reheat.
perfect, that works. scoreboard: dad 1, sleep 0. thanks
Nice work, dad. Send it off and see if you can sneak in a nap when the baby does. Good luck with the dinner!

Congrats on getting him down. Here are some ways to eat in peace without missing a wake-up:

**Monitoring**
- **Keep the monitor within reach and the volume up.** Put it on the table next to you, not across the room. If it's a video monitor, check that the screen is on and the audio alerts are enabled.
- **Eat close by.** If you can, sit where you'd hear him even without the monitor, like the kitchen table instead of in front of the TV.
- **Keep the TV low or use subtitles.** Background noise is the most common reason people miss the first fussy sounds.

**Timing**
- **Pick food that's ready fast.** Leftovers or something you can heat in one go mean you're not standing at the stove during the riskiest window.
- **Start the microwave or oven before you put him down**, if you can, so dinner is ready the moment you're free. If not, heat it right away while the room is quiet.
- **Remember the first 10-20 minutes can be light sleep.** He may stir or fuss as he settles. Give him a minute or two before going in, since many babies resettle on their own.

**Safety**
- **Don't walk away from anything on the stove or in the oven.** Set a timer on your phone.
- **Set a phone alarm for 20-30 minutes** as a backup check if you're worried about dozing off or getting absorbed in something.

**Eat first, clean up later.** Leave the dishes until after you've had your food, and go for the hot meal while it's hot.

Enjoy the quiet. Hope dinner's a good one.

**Set up your ears**
- Use a baby monitor, or the audio on the shared tracker app if it has one, and keep the volume where you can hear a fuss but not every rustle.
- Eat close to his room, ideally within a few steps, so you can get there fast even if the monitor drops out.

**Make dinner quick and low-effort**
- Pick something that reheats in a few minutes and can be eaten with one hand if needed, like frozen meals or leftover chili over rice.
- Plate it before you sit so you aren't getting up for anything.

- Babies often stir and resettle on their own. Give him 60 to 90 seconds before going in, and check the monitor for whether it's a real cry or just a squawk.
- If he does wake, a hand on his chest and a low hum may be enough, so you can get back to your plate.
- Keep the food easy to pause: cover it, or put it somewhere you can return to without it getting cold or messy.

**If you're alone**
- If Hana is home, tell her you're eating so one of you is on call.

Enjoy it, and I hope the crib holds for the whole meal. 🙃

I don't have your return date, your baby's age, or what childcare setup you've chosen, so I've built this around a countdown from the date you go back. Tell me the date and I'll turn the weeks into real calendar dates and cut anything that doesn't apply.

**How to use it:** Find how many weeks you have left and start at that row. If you have less time than the list assumes, squeeze the earlier weeks together and keep the order.

---

## 6+ weeks out: Foundations
- Confirm your exact return date and schedule with your employer (hours, remote or hybrid days, flexibility in the first couple of weeks).
- Ask HR about pumping policy: a private space, break times, and a fridge for milk.
- Lock in childcare: signed contract, start date, fees, and closure days.
- Get daycare paperwork started: enrollment forms, immunization records, and doctor's forms, which can take a while.
- Sort out a backup care plan for sick days (family, a backup sitter, or flexible work days).
- Review budget changes: childcare costs, benefits changes, and a dependent care FSA if available.

## 5 weeks out: Pump and bottle groundwork
- If you're breastfeeding, get your pump ready: check your insurance for a covered pump, and buy extra flanges, valves, and storage bags.
- Introduce a bottle if you haven't already. Having someone other than you offer it often goes better.
- Ask daycare for their bottle and milk policy in writing: labeling, how much to send, storage and warming rules, and how they handle formula.
- Start a small freezer stash, even a few ounces a day.

## 4 weeks out: Practice runs begin
- Try a few different bottle nipple types if baby resists.
- Have a caregiver (partner, grandparent) do a few bottle feeds while you're out of the room.
- Visit daycare again if possible, and ask about their daily routine, nap setup, and how they communicate during the day.
- Order what daycare requires: labeled bottles, spare clothes, sleep sack, pacifiers, and a bag.
- Plan your work wardrobe. Things may fit differently, and it's easier to sort now than the night before.

## 3 weeks out: Routines
- Start shifting baby toward the daycare schedule: wake-up, naps, and feeding times.
- Do a trial morning routine, timing everything from wake-up to door.
- Settle who does drop-off and pick-up on which days.
- Plan how you'll split sick-day duty with your partner.
- Check in with your manager about your first-week workload and any training or onboarding you need.

## 2 weeks out: Dress rehearsals
- Do a full practice day: get out the door on time, drive or commute the route, and leave baby with a caregiver for several hours.
- Check that baby takes bottles from the daycare-style setup (the bottle brand, the amount, and the person).
- Label everything and pack a test daycare bag.
- Prepare grab-and-go meals for the first week or two.
- Do a work tech check: logins, VPN, email access, and any required training you can finish early.

## 1 week out: Final prep
- Confirm start date, drop-off time, and any orientation or settling-in days with daycare.
- Fill the freezer stash to your target. Daycare usually needs a day or two of milk to start, plus extra for emergencies.
- Pack the bag and lay out outfits.
- Do laundry and set out the first week's meals.
- Review your pumping schedule so it fits around meetings.
- Add daycare and backup contacts to both parents' phones.
- Schedule something for yourself in the first week, like a walk or a coffee with a friend.

## The last 2-3 days
- Final bottle check: wash and label everything.
- Pack your own work bag, including pump parts, cooler, and a spare shirt.
- Prepare the morning-of: outfits, bags by the door, and car loaded if possible.
- Go to bed early.

## First day back
- Allow extra time for drop-off, and keep the goodbye short and warm.
- Put your phone on for daycare calls but don't plan to check in constantly.
- Pump on schedule and note the output.

Cereal at 9pm is a very common outcome of the witching hour. The fix is mostly to take dinner out of the 5-7pm chaos, not to cook faster during it.

**Shift the work earlier**
- **Cook during naptime or in the morning.** Even 15 minutes of chopping or browning meat at 10am or 1pm changes the evening completely. By 5pm you're only reheating or assembling.
- **Slow cooker or Instant Pot.** Dump everything in at lunchtime, and dinner is done when the fussiness starts. Chili, shredded chicken, pulled pork, and soups are all forgiving.
- **Sheet-pan meals.** Toss protein and veg on a pan, then oven for 25 minutes with almost no attention. You can prep it earlier and keep it in the fridge.

**Lower the bar for "actual dinner"**
- Dinner can be a rotisserie chicken, a bagged salad, and microwave rice. That counts.
- Keep 3-4 "assemble, don't cook" meals on rotation: quesadillas, pasta with jarred sauce and frozen meatballs, egg scrambles with toast and fruit, snack-plate dinners (cheese, crackers, cucumbers, hummus, deli meat).
- Stock the freezer with things that go from freezer to plate: dumplings, frozen veg, fish sticks, burritos, soup you made in a big batch.

**Handle the baby during the crunch**
- Wear the baby or use a carrier if they tolerate it, even for just 15 minutes of cooking.
- Put the baby somewhere safe where they can see you, like a bouncer or a high chair at the counter, with something to look at.
- Save a special "witching hour only" toy or activity so it stays interesting.

**Make the 9pm backup less sad**
- If you do end up late, a low-effort upgrade like toast with eggs, or pasta with butter and parmesan, takes 10 minutes and beats cereal.
- Take turns: one person holds the baby while the other puts something together.

Here's a checklist for that classic ~40-minute wake-up. It often means he's finishing his first sleep cycle and struggling to link into the next one, so the goal is to make the environment and routine as consistent as possible.

**Room environment**
- **Darkness:** Make it pitch black. Check for light leaks around the curtains and cover any glowing LEDs.
- **Temperature:** Aim for about 68-72°F (20-22°C). A room that's too warm or cooling off overnight can cause wakings.
- **White noise:** Run it continuously all night, not on a timer. If it shuts off, he may wake when the sound changes. Keep it at a moderate volume, about the level of a shower, and place it away from his head.
- **Airflow and dryness:** Check for drafts, and consider a humidifier if the air is dry.

**Sleepwear and sleep surface**
- **Layers:** Check that he isn't too hot or too cold. His chest and back should feel warm but not sweaty.
- **Sleep sack or swaddle:** Make sure it fits properly and isn't too tight or loose. If he's rolling or startling, adjust accordingly.
- **Mattress and sheet:** Look for wrinkles, damp spots, or anything uncomfortable. Make sure the diaper is holding up through the night.

**Timing**
- **Bedtime:** Both overtired and undertired can cause an early wake. If he wakes crying or frantic, try moving bedtime 15-20 minutes earlier. If he wakes alert and happy, try a bit later.
- **Last wake window:** Check that the stretch before bed isn't too long or too short for his age.
- **Naps:** Too little daytime sleep can lead to an overtired baby, while a late or long last nap can leave him not tired enough.

**Feeding**
- **Full feeds before bed:** Make sure he's getting enough during the evening, and consider a full feed as part of the bedtime routine.
- **Hunger or growth spurts:** Wakings that suddenly start can be hunger or a developmental leap.

**Bedtime routine**
- **Consistency:** Keep a short, predictable sequence (bath, feed, book, song) in the same order every night.
- **Drowsy but awake:** If he's fully asleep when you put him down, he may be disoriented when he surfaces at the end of the first cycle. Putting him down a bit more awake can help him learn to link cycles.
- **Same conditions at waking:** If he falls asleep with something (rocking, feeding, pacifier), he may expect it again when he wakes.

**Health and comfort**
- **Teething, congestion, reflux, or an ear infection** can all cause wakings. Check for drooling, fussing, or a stuffy nose.
- **Motor skill milestones:** Rolling, sitting, or pulling up can disrupt sleep for a while.

**Response**
- **Pause before going in:** Give him 3-5 minutes to see if he resettles himself.
- **Keep it low-key:** Dim lights, minimal talking, and the same soothing steps each time.

**Tracking**
- For 3-4 nights, jot down bedtime, wake time, what the wake sounded like (cry vs. fuss), room temperature, and what helped. Patterns usually show up quickly.

Waking about 40 minutes after bedtime is a really common spot to get stuck. It's usually the end of the first sleep cycle, where he comes up lightly and can't link into the next one. Here's a checklist, roughly from easiest to most involved.

**Environment**
- [ ] Room is dark enough. Hold your hand up at the crib, and if you can see details, add blackout curtains or tape over LED lights.
- [ ] White noise on "rain" runs all night at a steady volume, not on a timer. A machine shutting off mid-night is a classic 40-minute waker. Keep it a safe distance from the crib.
- [ ] Room temperature is comfortable (roughly 68-72°F), and he's dressed for it in a sleep sack.
- [ ] Nothing in the crib except a fitted sheet.
- [ ] Check the Wi-Fi monitor. If it's dropping connection or lighting up, it can add noise or light. Also keep the microwave off while he's in his first sleep stretch, since the dropout may make you go in when he's actually fine.

**Falling asleep**
- [ ] Put him down drowsy but awake, not fully asleep, so he doesn't wake in a different situation from the one he fell asleep in.
- [ ] Use the same wind-down every night, ending with the hummed tune, in the same order.
- [ ] Check the gap between nap 3 and bedtime. If he's overtired or undertired at bedtime, the first cycle gets choppy. If the 4:00 nap runs long, bedtime may need to shift a bit later, and if it's short, a bit earlier.
- [ ] Make sure the last feed is full and happens at the start of the routine, not as the last step before the crib.

**When he wakes**
- [ ] Pause 2-3 minutes before going in. He may resettle on his own.
- [ ] If you go in, start light: a hand on his chest, shushing, or the hum, before picking him up.
- [ ] Note whether he's hungry, wet or just stirring. If it's true hunger, a small top-up is fine. Just keep it low-key and dim.

**Track it for a few nights**
- [ ] Log bedtime, exact wake time, and what helped. Compare it with the 4:00 nap length and the evening crying stretch. One note per night is enough, since it takes a few nights to see a pattern.

Waking every 2 hours for a few nights fits the early 4-month sleep change. Sleep cycles are maturing around now, and it can start a few weeks before 4 months. It's also worth ruling out other causes first. Here's a plan for next week.

**Step 1: Rule out other causes (Sat-Sun)**

| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Illness/teething | Fever, congestion, pulling at ears, heavy drooling |
| Hunger | Is he taking full feeds, especially in the evening? Does he cluster feed? |
| Growth spurt | Extra hungry for a few days, then it settles |
| Environment | Room dark, white noise steady, temperature comfortable |
| Overtired | Is nap 3 running late or short? |

Call the pediatrician if there's fever, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or a cry that sounds different from his usual one.

**Step 2: Daily plan (Mon-Sun)**

| Area | What to do |
|---|---|
| Naps | Keep the 9, 12:30 and 4 anchors. Protect total daytime sleep, because overtired babies wake more at night. |
| Last nap | Keep it short and end it by about 4:45 so bedtime isn't pushed back. |
| Bedtime routine | Do the same 15-20 minute sequence every night: feed, quiet song, dim room. |
| Night wakings | Wait 1-2 minutes before going in. Many babies resettle on their own. |
| Feeds | Feed only if he's truly hungry. Keep the lights low and don't chat. |
| Putting him down | Drowsy but awake when you can, so he practices falling asleep in the crib. |
| Don't start new habits | Avoid anything you won't want to keep, like rocking to sleep every time. |

**Step 3: Split the night between you and Hana**

| Shift | Who | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Evening to 2am | You (or Hana, trade nights) | Protect one 4-5 hour stretch of real sleep for the off-duty parent. Earplugs help. |
| 2am | You | Keep your current feed. |
| 5am | Hana | Keep her current feed. |
| Mon-Thu | Judith | Have her cover the morning nap so you can catch up on sleep. |
| Fri-Sun | Just you and Hana | Take turns sleeping in. Decide who gets which morning before Friday at 5. |

**Step 4: Track it (5 minutes a day)**
Add three columns to your summary tab: number of wakings, longest stretch, and what settled him. Review after 7 days. If it's a regression, expect it to last 2-6 weeks. A single bad night means little. A trend does.

**Quiz:** Suppose his nights get worse for three days, but his daytime naps stay exactly on schedule. What would you check first, and why? Guess before you look at your log.

I don't have anything on file about Theo's age, feeding, or sleep setup, so I'm going on what you've told me: frequent waking every ~2 hours, and you suspect the 4-month regression. Adjust anything that doesn't fit.

## First, a quick reality check
- The "4-month sleep regression" is really a permanent maturing of sleep cycles (more adult-like light and deep sleep stages). It often shows up anywhere from about 3 to 5 months, so early is normal.
- Before assuming regression, rule out the usual overlapping causes: growth spurt (extra hunger), a developmental leap (rolling, new sounds), teething, congestion or illness, a room that's too warm or too bright, and swaddle issues if he's starting to roll.
- If there's fever, pulling at ears, unusual fussiness, feeding refusal, or fewer wet diapers, call the pediatrician rather than waiting it out.

## Next week's plan

**Daytime (the biggest lever)**
- Aim for a consistent wake-up time each morning (within ~30 min).
- Watch wake windows: at this age roughly 1.5 to 2 hours. Overtired babies wake more at night.
- Total daytime sleep is usually about 3 to 4 hours across 3 to 4 naps. Try to avoid very short catnaps stacking up late in the day.
- Offer full feeds during the day (distraction-free if he's getting easily pulled off), so he's not making up calories at night.
- Get daylight exposure in the morning and keep the evening dim.

**Bedtime routine**
- 20 to 30 minutes, same order every night: feed, bath or wipe-down, pajamas, book or song, lights low.
- Bedtime roughly 7:00 to 8:00 pm, moving earlier if he's been overtired.
- Put him down drowsy but awake some of the time if you're comfortable with that. It helps him practice linking sleep cycles. No need to be rigid about it.

**Sleep environment**
- Dark room (blackout curtains), white noise at a low steady volume, around 68 to 72°F.
- If he's started rolling, stop swaddling arms-in and move to a sleep sack.
- Firm flat surface, nothing loose in the crib.

**Night wakings**
- Pause 2 to 3 minutes before responding. Babies often fuss between cycles and resettle on their own.
- If he needs you, start with the least stimulating help: a hand on his chest, shushing, then picking up if needed.
- Feed if he's genuinely hungry (it's still normal at this age), but keep it quiet and dim, with no play and no talking.
- If he's feeding every 2 hours, try to space things slightly: a comfort-first approach before the bottle or breast, then a full feed.
- Keep things boring so he learns nights are for sleeping.

## Day-by-day rhythm
- **Mon to Tue:** Set the wake time, wake windows, and routine. Don't change anything else.
- **Wed to Thu:** Watch for patterns (which wake is the hungry one, which is the habit one). Jot down times.
- **Fri to Sun:** Adjust bedtime up or down 15 to 30 min based on what you saw. Try the gentle pause approach at the wakings that seem non-hunger.

## For you
- Trade off night shifts with a partner if you can, so each of you gets one protected 4 to 5 hour stretch.
- Nap when he does if you're running on empty. This phase usually settles in 2 to 6 weeks once he adapts.
- Don't introduce new sleep crutches you wouldn't want to keep.

## When to reassess
If it's still every 2 hours after about 10 to 14 days of consistency, or he seems unwell or isn't gaining well, check in with your pediatrician.

If you tell me his exact age, how he's fed, and what his current naps and bedtime look like, I can tailor the schedule down to specific times.

Frequent waking at about 3.5 months is very common, and the "4-month regression" often starts a few weeks early. It's a permanent change in how his sleep cycles work (more adult-like light and deep phases), so the goal is to build good habits around it rather than wait it out.

## What's likely going on
- Sleep cycles are maturing, so he surfaces more often between cycles.
- Wake-ups every ~2 hours fit this, but check the other causes below first.
- It typically lasts 2-6 weeks, though the new sleep pattern itself sticks around.

## Rule out other causes first (this weekend)
| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Hunger | Is he feeding well during the day? Growth spurts around now can mean extra night feeds |
| Comfort | Room temperature, clothing, wet diaper at wake-ups |
| Illness or teething | Fever, congestion, unusual fussing, drooling. Call the pediatrician if any of these show up |
| Environment | Noise or disruptions around the wake-ups (the 2 a.m. stretch may overlap with neighbor noise or Wi-Fi drops on the monitor) |

## Plan for next week
| Area | What to do |
|---|---|
| Naps | Keep your 9 / 12:30 / 4 schedule. Don't cut daytime sleep. Overtiredness makes night waking worse |
| Last wake window | Keep the window before bed at ~90 minutes or slightly shorter. If he's fussy, move bedtime earlier rather than later |
| Bedtime routine | Same 15-20 minute sequence each night: feed, dim lights, song, crib. Consistency matters more than the specifics |
| Night wakes | Pause 1-2 minutes before going in. Many wakes resolve on their own |
| Night feeds | Feed if he's actually hungry, but keep it dim and quiet. Skip talking and play |
| Drowsy but awake | Practice putting him down sleepy but not fully asleep, at least for the first sleep of the night |
| Sleep environment | Keep white noise steady all night. Make the room dark. Stop swaddling if he shows signs of rolling |
| Logging | Add a "night wakes" column to your tracker: time, duration, fed or not, what settled him |

## Splitting the work
| Days | Who covers |
|---|---|
| Mon-Fri | Keep your 2 a.m. / Hana 5 a.m. split. Judith is there during the day, so one of you can nap while she's on duty |
| Sat-Sun | Just the two of you, so trade nights: one person takes all wake-ups while the other sleeps with earplugs. Switch Sunday |

## Expectations
- Don't judge progress night to night. Look at the weekly trend in your log.
- Skip big changes (like sleep training or dropping a nap) in the middle of the regression.
- Some nights will be rough regardless. That's the regression, not a failure of the schedule.

## When to call the pediatrician
- Fever, vomiting, or fewer wet diapers
- Poor feeding or poor weight gain
- A cry that sounds different or can't be soothed
- Waking that's getting worse after 4-6 weeks

If you paste a few nights from the tracker next week, we can read the wake times the way we did with the naps and see whether there's a pattern.

Waking every 2 hours at 3.5 months can be the early edge of the 4-month sleep shift. That window usually runs from about 3.5 to 4.5 months, so "early" is within normal. It's temporary, but it's worth ruling out a few other causes first.

## 1. Quick checks this weekend

| Check | What to look for | If yes |
|---|---|---|
| Hunger or growth spurt | Eager, frantic feeding; more daytime feeds | Feed him. Add a feed in the late afternoon or evening |
| Overtired | Wake windows creeping past ~90-120 min, or short naps | Pull nap 3 earlier or add a brief catnap |
| Rolling or new skills | Rolling, kicking, flipping in the crib | Stop swaddling if you still do. Give him floor practice time by day |
| Illness or teething | Fever, drooling, gnawing, pulling at ears, congestion | Call Dr. Fong if there's a fever or feeding or diaper changes |
| Environment | Room too warm or bright, white noise cutting out | Keep the room dark and cool, and keep 'rain' steady all night |

## 2. Daytime foundation (keep it simple)

| Piece | Plan |
|---|---|
| Naps | Keep the 9, 12:30 and 4 schedule, but treat it as a guide rather than a pass/fail test. A regression can scramble a good day. |
| Morning walk | Keep the boardwalk walk before nap 1 if it's working. Daylight helps regulate sleep. |
| Full feeds | Aim for full feeds during the day so he isn't making up calories at night. |
| Evening | Same short wind-down every night: feed, dim room, hum the ballpark tune, then crib. |

## 3. Night-wake protocol

1. Pause 2-3 minutes before going in. He may resettle on his own.
2. If he's hungry (as opposed to just stirring), feed him, keep the lights low and don't chat.
3. If he's not hungry, try shushing or a hand on the chest before picking him up.
4. Put him down drowsy but awake when you can. Don't stress if he falls asleep during the feed.
5. If the monitor drops when the microwave runs, check the audio, not a sprint. The camera should reconnect on its own.

## 4. Splitting the load with Hana

| When | Plan |
|---|---|
| Sat-Sun | Judith's away, so it's just the two of you. Keep the 2 a.m./5 a.m. split, and let whoever had the rougher night nap during one of his naps. |
| Mon-Fri | Judith's back at 8 on Monday. Hand her the morning nap and lunch while you sleep for a 60-90 minute stretch. |
| If nights get worse | Switch to a "whoever is up first" pattern for a few nights. Don't both stay up. |

## 5. Don't overbuild this

You don't need a new spreadsheet. In the tracker app, just note the number of wakes and what fixed them. Three or four nights of notes are enough to spot a pattern, and Dr. Fong can use them on Nov 19.

## 6. When to call sooner

Call the pediatrician if you see a fever, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, vomiting, a different-sounding cry, or if he can't be soothed at all.

Regressions usually last 2-6 weeks. You're not doing something wrong, and it doesn't mean the schedule you built has failed. Do you want a one-page version for the fridge, or a cheat-sheet version for Hana?

full_context.text:
Theo is about 3.5 months, so this isn't early. The 4-month sleep change usually shows up anywhere from 3.5 to 4.5 months. It's a permanent reorganization of his sleep cycles, so the goal is to stay consistent through it rather than fix it.

**1. Rule things out first (this weekend)**

| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Illness | Temp (100.4°F or higher means call the nurse line), congestion, ear tugging |
| Hunger / growth spurt | Taking more oz than usual, or waking hungry |
| Rolling or new skills | Practicing in the crib, startling awake |
| Environment | Room temp around 68-72°F, white noise steady, room dark |

If any of these point to something, call Dr. Fong's office rather than treating it as regression.

**2. Keep the daytime anchors steady**

| Item | Plan |
|---|---|
| Naps | Keep the crib naps at about 9, 12:30 and 4 |
| Wake windows | About 90 minutes, stretching toward 100-105 minutes only if he falls asleep easily |
| Last nap | Cap it at 45-60 minutes and wake him by 5:00 so bedtime isn't pushed |
| Evening | Start the same wind-down each night and hum the ballpark organ tune as the sleep cue |
| Daytime feeds | Full feeds during the day so he isn't making up calories at night |

**3. Night-waking protocol (use the same steps every time)**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Wait 60-90 seconds, since he may resettle on his own |
| 2 | If he escalates, use a hand on his chest, shushing and the tune, with no lights or talking |
| 3 | Check the basics: diaper, gas, temperature |
| 4 | Feed only if it's close to a normal feed time or he's clearly hungry. Otherwise settle without feeding |
| 5 | If he's still wound up after about 10 minutes, pick him up briefly, then put him back down drowsy but awake |

Try to avoid starting new sleep habits this week, like rocking to sleep every time. That's the hardest pattern to undo later.

**4. Who covers what**

| When | Plan |
|---|---|
| Sat-Sun | Just you and Hana, so trade nap duty and give the 5-8 p.m. stretch two 90-minute blocks. Decide tonight who sleeps in Saturday |
| Mon-Fri | You keep the 2 a.m. feed and Hana the 5 a.m., and Judith covers daytime from 8. Tell her the night-waking steps so she follows the same ones at naps |
| Monitor | The camera drops when the microwave runs, so warm bottles with the mug of hot water trick during waking stretches. That way a dropout doesn't send you sprinting |

**5. Track it (5 minutes a day)**

| Log | Why |
|---|---|
| Each wake-up time and how long to resettle | Shows whether it's improving |
| Total night sleep and longest stretch | Tells you whether it's regression or just a bad night |
| Day nap lengths | Short naps feed into worse nights |

Bring the log to the Nov 19 visit at 9:40, since sleep is already on your question list.

**6. Call the pediatrician if**
- He has a fever of 100.4°F or higher
- He refuses several feeds or has fewer wet diapers than usual
- He cries inconsolably or the cry sounds different from usual
- Waking is paired with labored breathing or vomiting

Expect this to last roughly 2-6 weeks. A few rough nights don't mean the schedule failed. Get some sleep when you can this weekend, and check in if you want to adjust the plan midweek.

Giving a concrete reason (muscle memory, one-handed access, sleep deprivation) tends to land better than "please don't touch my stuff," because it's about your system working, not about her doing something wrong.

**2. Give her an alternative outlet.**
People who reorganize are often looking for a way to feel useful. Offer her a task that's hers: "Can you be in charge of restocking wipes and diapers?" or "Want to set up the laundry corner however you like?" That gives her a space to organize without touching yours.

**3. Make the setup visible and intentional.**
A small label, a basket with a clear purpose, or even telling her "this is set up for night changes, so please leave it" can signal that it's not random. It's a bit of a boundary marker without being a confrontation.

**4. Ask what she was fixing.**
Three times in a row suggests she sees something that bugs her. If she says "the wipes were too far from the changing pad," you might find a tweak that works for both of you, or at least understand where it's coming from.

If you do move it back tonight, that's fine, but I'd pair it with a quick conversation tomorrow so you're not just resetting it on repeat. It's also totally reasonable to be annoyed. Having your space rearranged while you're running on little sleep is frustrating, even when the intent is kind.

Not witchcraft, though there's no single magic ingredient. The "grandma effect" is usually a bundle of things that are reproducible in pieces:

**Why it works at grandma's**
- **Different person, different expectations.** Kids often settle faster for someone who isn't their usual source of negotiation. There's less history of "if I protest, mom caves."
- **Calm, unhurried energy.** A grandparent with no agenda that afternoon tends to be more relaxed than a parent juggling ten other things. Kids read that.
- **Novelty plus routine.** A new environment can make a kid tired from taking it all in, while a consistent ritual (same blanket, book, white noise) provides the cue to sleep.
- **Consistency of the person.** Grandma doing it the same way every time makes it predictable.
- **Wear-down beforehand.** Grandma's place often means more stimulation, snacks, attention, and sometimes outdoor time, so he may just be more tired.

**What you can copy at home**
- A short, identical pre-nap ritual, done the same way each time
- Matching darkness, sound, and temperature to wherever he sleeps well
- A flat, boring, confident tone: no bargaining, no multiple "last" requests
- Having the other parent or a different adult handle the put-down for a while
- Good activity or outside time beforehand

**What you can't fully copy**
- The novelty, and the fact that grandma isn't the parent. Some of the effect is simply that you aren't the one he's testing.

**Tips for the trial run**
- Ask your mom to follow his usual routine at first, and send her his cues: what he does when tired, his comfort items, and typical wake windows.
- Bring his sleep stuff (lovey, sleep sack, white noise machine) so the sleep setup feels familiar.
- Do a shorter visit first, maybe just one nap, before an overnight.
- Expect it might go either way. Some kids nap great there, others hold out for home.

If it goes well, ask your mom what she actually did. Her answer is probably more useful than any theory.

Not witchcraft, though it's less magic than it looks. Grandma-house naps usually go well for a handful of ordinary reasons, and most of them can be copied at home:

| Likely factor | What's going on | Can you reproduce it? |
|---|---|---|
| One calm adult, no handoffs | Babies often settle better when one person is fully focused on them | Yes: one person on nap duty, phones away |
| Novelty | A new place, new smells and a new voice can make a baby more alert, or sometimes more soothed | Partly: a new spot works briefly, but the effect fades |
| Motion and holding | Grandparents tend to hold, rock or walk longer, and contact naps run longer | Yes, but it can become a habit |
| Relaxed timing | Less clock-watching, so the nap starts when he's actually ready | Yes: watch his cues and keep his 90-minute windows |
| Different cues | Different light, sound and routine can make a baby less (or more) fussy | Yes: white noise, dark room, same pre-nap routine |
| Fresh energy | Someone rested and unhurried is calmer, and babies pick up on that | Hardest, since you're running on broken sleep |

That last one is probably the biggest factor. It's not that you're doing anything wrong. A rested, unhurried person is just easier for a baby to settle with.

**For the condo trip:**
- Bring his sleep setup: white noise, sleep sack, and the same pre-nap routine. A portable crib that smells like home helps.
- Share his nap times (9, 12:30, 4) and wake windows, but be ready for his schedule to wobble a bit. One off day doesn't mean much.
- Ask for a short log of when he slept and for how long, so you can compare it with your tracker.
- Don't expect a perfect result. Some babies sleep worse in a new place, and a trial run for an hour or two is a good test before a longer stretch.

If it does go better there, that's useful information, not a verdict on you. You can borrow the parts that transfer, like the calmer pacing and the consistent routine.

Want a one-page handoff sheet for your mom with his schedule and soothing steps?

Probably a bit of both: it's less witchcraft than "a bundle of small differences that add up." And some of it you can copy at home.

**What's likely behind it**
- **Novelty and a different caregiver.** Some babies settle faster for someone who is calm, unhurried, and not their own parent. Babies pick up on tension, and a long day on duty can leak through. Grandma isn't running on 2 a.m. feeds.
- **Her environment.** The condo is probably quieter, with different light, temperature, and sound. Your place has a tiny kitchen, a microwave that drops the camera, a neighbor in 211, and the evening crying stretch.
- **Her routine.** If she's consistent about timing, the room, and how she puts him down, that matters more than any one trick.
- **Fresh energy.** Daytime naps at someone else's place often go well because the baby is a bit more curious and tired from the change.

**What you can copy at home**
- **Same sequence every time:** a short wind-down, the same words or song, then down while drowsy but awake.
- **Room setup:** dark, cool (about 68-72°F), white noise at a steady volume. You already have the machine on rain, so check that it's not too quiet or too loud.
- **A calm handoff:** whoever does the put-down goes in relaxed, with no rushing or hovering.
- **Ask her what she does.** She may be doing small things she doesn't think count, like how she holds him, the pace, or where she stands.

**What not to copy**
Dr. Fong advised stopping the swaddle, and Theo is starting to roll. If any of her magic involves swaddling, it's worth checking the sleep setup together rather than quietly redoing it. A simple "Dr. Fong asked us to stop swaddling, so what else do you do that works?" keeps it about the baby, not about her.

**For the condo trial**
- Try one daytime nap or a few hours first, not a full overnight.
- Send his usual white noise, his sleep sack, and a note with his nap times (9, 12:30, 4) so the schedule doesn't drift.
- Log it as a separate location in the tracker so you can compare it with home naps without making it a big project.
- If it goes great, treat it as a bonus. If it flops, one nap at a new place doesn't tell you much either way.

Hana gets a real break, and you may learn something about what works at home. If you'd like, I can draft the note for your mom or a short nap handoff sheet.

Here's a quick checklist of typical 4-month milestones. Babies vary a lot, so treat these as general markers rather than deadlines.

**Social and emotional**
- Smiles spontaneously, especially at people
- Enjoys playing with others and may cry when play stops
- Copies some movements and expressions (smiling, frowning)

**Communication**
- Coos and makes sounds like "oooo" and "aahh"
- Babbles with expression, sometimes "talks back" when you talk to them
- Cries differently for hunger, tiredness, or discomfort
- Turns head toward voices

**Vision and thinking**
- Follows moving objects with their eyes
- Watches faces closely and recognizes familiar people
- Reaches for toys and brings hands to mouth
- Shows interest in bright colors and patterns

**Movement**
- Holds head steady without support
- Pushes up onto elbows or forearms during tummy time
- Pushes down with legs when feet are on a firm surface
- May roll from tummy to back
- Opens and shuts hands, swipes at dangling objects

**Worth mentioning to the pediatrician**
- Doesn't follow moving objects with eyes
- Doesn't smile at people
- Can't hold head up or doesn't bring hands to mouth
- Doesn't respond to loud sounds
- Seems very stiff or very floppy
- Loses skills they previously had

If something feels off, trust your instincts and bring it up at the next checkup. Early check-ins are never wasted.

Here's a general checklist for around 4 months. Babies vary a lot, so treat it as a guide, not a test.

| Area | Typical milestones |
|---|---|
| Social/emotional | Smiles at people on purpose, laughs, enjoys play, may cry when play stops |
| Communication | Coos and babbles, makes sounds back to you, turns toward voices, different cries for hunger, tiredness or discomfort |
| Movement | Holds head steady without support, pushes up on forearms during tummy time, brings hands to mouth, may roll from tummy to back, pushes down on legs when held standing |
| Vision/hearing | Follows moving objects with his eyes, watches faces, reaches for or swipes at dangling toys, startles at loud sounds |
| Thinking | Shows interest in his hands, recognizes familiar people, may show boredom or excitement |

**Worth mentioning to the pediatrician:** he doesn't follow things with his eyes, doesn't smile at people, doesn't bring hands to his mouth, can't hold his head up, doesn't respond to sounds, or seems to lose a skill he had. Since you just had the four-month visit with Dr. Fong, you can also ask her about anything you noticed that didn't come up.

Rolling attempts, which you've mentioned, fit right in the typical range. Tummy time is the best practice for most of the movement skills.
